claim: Humans and animals construct internal models of their environment in order to select appropriate courses of action.
source: Humans and animals construct internal models of their environment in order to select appropriate courses of action.
evidence: This is a general statement about cognitive processes that draws from established scientific understanding.

claim: The representation of uncertainty about the current state of the environment is a key feature of internal models that controls the rate of learning as well as directly affecting choice behaviour.
source: The representation of uncertainty about the current state of the environment is a key feature of these models that controls the rate of learning as well as directly affecting choice behaviour.
evidence: This statement reflects established theoretical understanding in the field of learning and decision-making.

claim: Most theoretical inference models include a dedicated mechanism to drive up model uncertainty to maintain flexibility.
source: To maintain flexibility, given that uncertainty naturally decreases over time, most theoretical inference models include a dedicated mechanism to drive up model uncertainty.
evidence: This is a statement about the structure of theoretical models in the field.

claim: Noradrenaline is involved in determining the uncertainty, or entropy, and thus flexibility, of neural models.
source: Here we probe the long-standing hypothesis that noradrenaline is involved in determining the uncertainty, or entropy, and thus flexibility, of neural models.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis being tested in the study.

claim: Pupil diameter indexes neuromodulatory state including noradrenaline release.
source: Pupil diameter, which indexes neuromodulatory state including noradrenaline release, predicted increases (but not decreases) in entropy in a neural state model encoded in human medial orbitofrontal cortex, as measured using multivariate functional MRI.
evidence: This is supported by citations in the manuscript and established knowledge in the field.

claim: Pupil diameter predicted increases (but not decreases) in entropy in a neural state model encoded in human medial orbitofrontal cortex.
source: Pupil diameter, which indexes neuromodulatory state including noradrenaline release, predicted increases (but not decreases) in entropy in a neural state model encoded in human medial orbitofrontal cortex, as measured using multivariate functional MRI.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on experimental data.

claim: Activity in anterior cingulate cortex predicted pupil diameter.
source: Activity in anterior cingulate cortex predicted pupil diameter.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on experimental data.

claim: The results provide evidence for top-down, neuromodulatory control of entropy in neural state models.
source: These results provide evidence for top-down, neuromodulatory control of entropy in neural state models.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: The current state of the environment can be thought of as a latent variable in internal models that cannot be observed directly but must be inferred from sensory observations.
source: The current state of the environment can be thought of as a latent variable in such models, that is a variable that cannot be observed directly but must be inferred from sensory observations.
evidence: This is a theoretical concept from the field of inference and learning.

claim: Theoretical accounts of inference tend to include two distinct processes for updating beliefs over time: evidence-driven updating and transition function updating.
source: Theoretical accounts of inference (sometimes called learning, as in reinforcement learning) tend to include two distinct processes for updating beliefs over time. The first process is evidence-driven updating of beliefs – after each new piece of evidence (such as a reward) is observed, the model is updated to take into account the new observation. The second process is one that occurs between observations, as states of the world for which no evidence has necessarily been observed are up-weighted to account for the possibility that the environment could change before the next observation.
evidence: This describes established theoretical frameworks in the field.

claim: Evidence-driven updating is driven by recently observed evidence and usually takes into account how that evidence differs from predictions under a prior belief.
source: Conceptually, evidence-driven updating, as the name suggests, is driven by recently observed evidence and usually takes into account how that evidence differs from predictions under a prior belief (e.g., reward prediction error).
evidence: This describes a theoretical concept in learning models.

claim: Updating under the transition function is driven by higher order features of the environment such as the inferred level of environmental volatility and structural knowledge about which environmental states tend to follow each other.
source: In contrast, updating under the transition function is driven by higher order features of the environment such as the inferred level of environmental volatility and structural knowledge about which environmental states tend to follow each other (Behrens et al., 2007; Meyniel and Dehaene, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The overall level and distribution of uncertainty in an internal model is controlled in part by the transition function.
source: Put another way, the overall level and distribution of uncertainty in an internal model is controlled in part by the transition function.
evidence: This is a theoretical statement about how internal models work.

claim: When the environment is believed to be changeable or to have recently changed, the transition function adjusts beliefs so that there is high uncertainty about the state of the world on trial t + 1.
source: When the environment is believed to be changeable (Behrens et al., 2007), or to have recently changed (Wilson et al., 2010), the transition function adjusts beliefs so that there is high uncertainty about the state of the world on trial t + 1, even given what was known at trial t.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The optimal level of uncertainty is determined by two opposing forces: if relatively little uncertainty is added at each transition the model can utilize a longer history of observations to infer the current state of the world; but if too little uncertainty is added, the model becomes inflexible.
source: The optimal level of uncertainty is determined by two opposing forces: if relatively little uncertainty is added at each transition the model can utilize a longer history of observations to infer the current state of the world; but if too little uncertainty is added, the model becomes inflexible.
evidence: This is a theoretical statement about optimal learning.

claim: Previous studies have observed BOLD and pupillometric signals tracking optimal uncertainty.
source: Furthermore, blood-oxygen-level dependent (BOLD) and pupillometric signals tracking such (optimal) uncertainty have been observed (Behrens et al., 2007; McGuire et al., 2014; Nassar et al., 2012; Preuschoff et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Behrens and colleagues argued that the learning rate should optimally depend on environmental volatility.
source: In relation to the first question, how the optimal level of uncertainty is calculated, Behrens and colleagues (Behrens et al., 2007) argued that the learning rate (analogous to the magnitude of the leak) should optimally depend on environmental volatility, and observed that when volatility (hence learning rate) was high, anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) was active.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: When volatility (hence learning rate) was high, anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) was active.
source: In relation to the first question, how the optimal level of uncertainty is calculated, Behrens and colleagues (Behrens et al., 2007) argued that the learning rate (analogous to the magnitude of the leak) should optimally depend on environmental volatility, and observed that when volatility (hence learning rate) was high, anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) was active.
evidence: This is a finding from a cited study.

claim: O'Reilly and colleagues showed activity in ACC when participants were instructed that changes in the environment had occurred.
source: O'Reilly and colleagues (O'Reilly et al., 2013) showed activity in a similar region when participants were instructed that changes in the environment had occurred.
evidence: This is a finding from a cited study.

claim: McGuire and colleagues found activity in ACC associated with belief uncertainty.
source: McGuire and colleagues (McGuire et al., 2014) found activity in ACC associated with belief uncertainty, another model-based measure that should determine the magnitude of the transition function (in their case, the probability that the model abandons its prior beliefs entirely in favour of a flat prior).
evidence: This is a finding from a cited study.

claim: Noradrenaline has been proposed as a candidate mechanism by which the level of uncertainty in neural models of the world may be controlled.
source: An intriguing possibility is that increases in neural model uncertainty are controlled via a neuromodulatory route. In particular noradrenaline has been proposed as a candidate mechanism by which the level of uncertainty in neural models of the world may be controlled (Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005; Bouret and Sara, 2005; Iigaya, 2016; Martins and Froemke, 2015; Nassar et al., 2012; Preuschoff et al., 2011; Pulcu and Browning, 2017; Yu and Dayan, 2005), and experimental manipulations increasing noradrenaline levels in cortex tend to lead to increased randomness in behavior (Tervo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Experimental manipulations increasing noradrenaline levels in cortex tend to lead to increased randomness in behavior.
source: An intriguing possibility is that increases in neural model uncertainty are controlled via a neuromodulatory route. In particular noradrenaline has been proposed as a candidate mechanism by which the level of uncertainty in neural models of the world may be controlled (Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005; Bouret and Sara, 2005; Iigaya, 2016; Martins and Froemke, 2015; Nassar et al., 2012; Preuschoff et al., 2011; Pulcu and Browning, 2017; Yu and Dayan, 2005), and experimental manipulations increasing noradrenaline levels in cortex tend to lead to increased randomness in behavior (Tervo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a finding from a cited study.

claim: One theoretical proposal is that noradrenaline performs a 'network reset'.
source: One theoretical proposal, that noradrenaline performs a 'network reset' (Bouret and Sara, 2005), is particularly reminiscent of the second, transition-function updating process described above.
evidence: This is a theoretical proposal from a cited study.

claim: In the 4-arm bandit task, at any given time, one of four response options had a high (70 or 90%) probability of delivering reward and the other three had a low (20%) probability.
source: At any given time, one of four response options had a high (70 or 90%) probability of delivering reward and the other three had a low (20%) probability.
evidence: This describes the experimental design of the task.

claim: The high reward option switched after a variable number of trials (mean 20 ± SD 5).
source: The high reward option switched after a variable number of trials (mean 20 ± SD 5).
evidence: This describes the experimental design of the task.

claim: Participants were explicitly instructed about the reward structure before beginning the task.
source: Participants were explicitly instructed about the reward structure before beginning the task.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: 72% of trials on average were classified as exploit trials.
source: 72% of trials on average were classified as exploit trials (SEM across participants 1.2%)
evidence: This is a behavioral result from the experiment.

claim: The mean length for an exploitation 'block' was 13.7 trials (across participants).
source: the mean length for an exploitation 'block' was 13.7 trials (across participants)
evidence: This is a behavioral result from the experiment.

claim: The within-subject standard deviation of exploitation block lengths was (mean across participants) 7.1 trials.
source: the within-subject standard deviation of exploitation block lengths was (mean across participants) 7.1 trials.
evidence: This is a behavioral result from the experiment.

claim: Model entropy was generally high in the exploit phases and low in the explore phases of the task.
source: Model entropy was generally high in the exploit phases and low in the explore phases of the task (Figure 1d,e)
evidence: This is a result from the model analysis, supported by figures.

claim: Model entropy tended to be higher when the pay-out rate of the high reward option was lower.
source: it also tended to be higher when the pay-out rate of the high reward option was lower.
evidence: This is a result from the model analysis.

claim: High entropy made it more likely that participants would switch from exploitation to exploration following a reward omission (t18 = 7.60, p=2.57×10−7).
source: Both high entropy, and high relative uncertainty, made it more likely that participants would switch from exploitation to exploration following a reward omission (two separate logistic regressions: entropy - t18 = 7.60, p=2.57×10−7; relative uncertainty - t18 = 13.50, p=3.7×10−11).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the behavioral analysis.

claim: High relative uncertainty made it more likely that participants would switch from exploitation to exploration following a reward omission (t18 = 13.50, p=3.7×10−11).
source: Both high entropy, and high relative uncertainty, made it more likely that participants would switch from exploitation to exploration following a reward omission (two separate logistic regressions: entropy - t18 = 7.60, p=2.57×10−7; relative uncertainty - t18 = 13.50, p=3.7×10−11).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the behavioral analysis.

claim: The explore phase engaged a frontal-parietal action network and the dorsomedial prefrontal cortex (dorsal anterior cingulate dACC and adjacent preSMA).
source: The explore phase engaged a frontal-parietal action network and the dorsomedial prefrontal cortex (dorsal anterior cingulate dACC and adjacent preSMA).
evidence: This is a result from the fMRI analysis (GLM1).

claim: The exploit phase engaged medial orbitofrontal cortex (mOFC) and the hippocampus.
source: The exploit phase engaged medial orbitofrontal cortex (mOFC) and the hippocampus, two regions known to be engaged in model-based choice (Boorman et al., 2016; Jones et al., 2012; Noonan et al., 2010; Wikenheiser et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a result from the fMRI analysis (GLM1), with citations supporting the interpretation.

claim: mOFC and hippocampus are two regions known to be engaged in model-based choice.
source: The exploit phase engaged medial orbitofrontal cortex (mOFC) and the hippocampus, two regions known to be engaged in model-based choice (Boorman et al., 2016; Jones et al., 2012; Noonan et al., 2010; Wikenheiser et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Response switching and high model entropy predicted activity throughout the frontal parietal network and dorsomedial frontal cortex.
source: Further analysis (GLM2, Figure 1—figure supplement 3) indicated that response switching and high model entropy (see below for details of model) predicted activity throughout the frontal parietal network and dorsomedial frontal cortex.
evidence: This is a result from the fMRI analysis (GLM2).

claim: Reward omission predicted activity in dorsomedial frontal cortex only.
source: Reward omission predicted activity in dorsomedial frontal cortex only, and reward activated ventral striatum.
evidence: This is a result from the fMRI analysis (GLM2).

claim: Reward activated ventral striatum.
source: Reward omission predicted activity in dorsomedial frontal cortex only, and reward activated ventral striatum.
evidence: This is a result from the fMRI analysis (GLM2).

claim: Low model entropy predicted activation of medial OFC and hippocampus.
source: Low model entropy predicted activation of medial OFC and hippocampus (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a result from the fMRI analysis (GLM2).

claim: Most of the differences in activity observed between exploitation and exploration were explained by task factors including entropy, response switching, and reward.
source: Most of the differences in activity observed between exploitation and exploration were explained by these factors (GLM3; Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a result from the fMRI analysis (GLM3).

claim: Core exploitation trials were defined as at least five trials after the last action switch and at least five trials before the next action switch.
source: By limiting our analysis to core exploitation trials (at least five trials, and therefore approximately twenty seconds, after the last action switch and at least five trials before the next action switch; such trials were 25% of all trials (mean across participants = 201/800 trials, SEM = 7.0)), we were able to identify neural activity concerned with changes in participants' beliefs in the absence of changes in overt behaviour.
evidence: This describes the analysis approach.

claim: Core exploitation trials were 25% of all trials (mean across participants = 201/800 trials, SEM = 7.0).
source: By limiting our analysis to core exploitation trials (at least five trials, and therefore approximately twenty seconds, after the last action switch and at least five trials before the next action switch; such trials were 25% of all trials (mean across participants = 201/800 trials, SEM = 7.0)), we were able to identify neural activity concerned with changes in participants' beliefs in the absence of changes in overt behaviour.
evidence: This is a result from the analysis.

claim: In the current task, state and option value are inherently interlinked because the possible states of the environment are simply the alternatives for which option is the high reward option.
source: However, it should be noted that in the current task, the possible states of the environment are simply the alternatives for which option is the high reward option, that is {option A is high reward option… option D is high reward option}. Thus, in the current task, state and option value are inherently interlinked.
evidence: This is an explanation of the task structure.

claim: High confidence in the currently chosen option (low entropy state) correlates with that option having a high expected value (mean correlation ± s.e.m: -0.93 ± 0.005).
source: It is necessarily the case that high confidence in the currently chosen option (low entropy state) correlates with that option having a high expected value (mean correlation ± s.e.m: -0.93 ± 0.005).
evidence: This is a result from the analysis showing the relationship between entropy and value.

claim: Recent studies have identified medial OFC as a likely site for a probabilistic model in the context of model-based reinforcement learning.
source: Recent studies have identified medial OFC as a likely site for such a probabilistic model in the context of model-based reinforcement learning (Chan et al., 2016; Schuck et al., 2016; Wilson et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The currently selected option can be decoded above chance in motor and visual cortex.
source: Simply searching for regions in which we could correctly classify the selected option, we were, as expected, able to decode at above-chance levels from a broad network of areas including motor and visual cortex (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is a result from the multivariate fMRI analysis.

claim: Decoding in visual cortex and motor cortex reveals a representational structure that is sensitive to spatial and motor factors.
source: A plot of the probability of decoding each action from visual cortex (Figure 2c, top) and motor cortex (Figure 2c, middle) reveals a representational structure that is sensitive to spatial and motor factors; the most likely options to be decoded, other than the actually selected option, are those corresponding to the chosen hand (and equivalently, the chosen visual hemifield).
evidence: This is a result from the multivariate fMRI analysis.

claim: Medial OFC represents the current state of the task probabilistically.
source: Medial OFC represents the current state of the task probabilistically.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the multivariate fMRI analysis (GLM4).

claim: The effect of model entropy on representation strength was also detectable in the hippocampus (t(18)=-2.11 p<0.05 uncorrected).
source: The same effect was also detectable in the hippocampus (t(18)=-2.11 p<0.05 uncorrected at an ROI centered on the peak voxel 34, -14, -16 for the exploit vs. explore univariate contrast from GLM 1; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a result from the multivariate fMRI analysis, though it did not survive correction for multiple comparisons.

claim: The effect in hippocampus did not survive whole brain correction for multiple comparisons and should be treated with caution.
source: However the effect in hippocampus did not survive whole brain correction for multiple comparisons and should therefore be treated with caution.
evidence: This is a caveat about the statistical significance of a result.

claim: The weighted representation of option preferences observed in mOFC is consistent with a probabilistic internal model of the environment.
source: The weighted representation of option preferences observed in mOFC is consistent with a probabilistic internal model of the environment, whereby the currently selected option has a higher decoding probability when model entropy is low (Figure 1b and Figure 2c, bottom).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the multivariate fMRI results.

claim: The mOFC representation is distinct from an action/policy representation, in which the representation of options is not modulated by entropy, as was observed in visual and motor areas.
source: It is distinct from an action/policy representation, in which the representation of options is not modulated by entropy, as was observed in visual and motor areas (Figure 2c, top and middle).
evidence: This is an interpretation comparing different brain regions.

claim: Using the probability assigned by the model that the currently exploited option is the high reward option as the predictor variable also produced a specific effect in the medial OFC.
source: To check that the result was specific to the current state of the environment, we repeated the above analysis but instead of model entropy, used the probability (belief) assigned by the model that the currently exploited option is the high reward option as the predictor variable (GLM5). This also produced a specific effect in the medial OFC (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a result from an alternative analysis (GLM5) confirming the main finding.

claim: When the pay-out rate of the exploited, high reward option was 90% vs. 70%, representation strength was higher in mOFC.
source: To confirm our result was not dependent on the particular learning model we used, we simply compared representation strength during exploit periods with high and low payout rates. When the pay-out rate of the exploited, high reward option was 90% vs. 70%, representation strength was higher in mOFC (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a result from an alternative analysis confirming the main finding.

claim: The effect of model entropy on representation strength remained significant after regressing out the effect of option value from univariate activity (t(18)=-7.62,p<0.001).
source: We examined whether our effects still held after regressing out a univariate effect of option value by repeating the analysis after first regressing out the effect of value from univariate activity in each voxel in the mOFC region of interest. The effect of model entropy on representation strength remained significant (t(18)=-7.62,p<0.001).
evidence: This is a result from a control analysis.

claim: The effect of model entropy on representation strength remained significant after regressing out recent reward history in addition to value (t(18)=-7.26,p<0.001).
source: This was also true when regressing out recent reward history (whether the current and previous three trials were rewarded) in addition to value (t(18)=-7.26,p<0.001) from voxelwise activity before carrying out multivariate analysis.
evidence: This is a result from a control analysis.

claim: Pupil size has primarily been interpreted in the literature as indexing noradrenaline levels, although the muscles controlling pupil size are sensitive to both noradrenaline and acetylcholine.
source: Pupil size has primarily been interpreted in the literature as indexing noradrenaline levels, although the muscles controlling pupil size are sensitive to both noradrenaline and acetylcholine.
evidence: This is a statement about the interpretation of pupil measurements in the literature.

claim: Changes in pupil diameter have been linked to single-unit activity in the (noradrenergic) LC.
source: Changes in pupil diameter have been linked to single-unit activity in the (noradrenergic) LC (Joshi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Both noradrenaline and acetylcholine as measured in cortex are associated with pupil size.
source: Recent physiological work has demonstrated that both noradrenaline and acetylcholine as measured in cortex, are associated with pupil size (Reimer et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Levels of both noradrenaline and acetylcholine were correlated with pupil dilation over a time course of up to a few seconds.
source: levels of both noradrenaline and acetylcholine were correlated with pupil dilation over a time course of up to a few seconds (a similar time course to the interval between trials in the current experiment).
evidence: This is based on cited work and inference about the time course.

claim: Noradrenaline, but not acetylcholine, was correlated with changes in pupil dilation (the temporal derivative of pupil size) as well as pupil size itself.
source: However, Reimer et al. (2016) also report that noradrenaline, but not acetylcholine, was correlated with changes in pupil dilation (the temporal derivative of pupil size) as well as pupil size itself, which favours a noradrenergic interpretation of our pupillometry results (most of the pupillometry results reported below concern changes in pupil size rather than pupil size per se).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Baseline pupil size was larger in explore than exploit trials.
source: Baseline pupil size was larger in explore than exploit trials (Figure 3a, left)
evidence: This is a result from the pupillometry analysis.

claim: Baseline pupil size increased when transitioning into exploration.
source: Baseline pupil size was larger in explore than exploit trials (Figure 3a, left), and increased when transitioning into exploration (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a result from the pupillometry analysis.

claim: Reward omission produced a sustained increase in pupil size following feedback.
source: On a trial-by-trial basis, reward omission produced a sustained increase in pupil size following feedback (Figure 3a, right).
evidence: This is a result from the pupillometry analysis.

claim: Changes in baseline pupil size explained changes in representation strength in mOFC on unrewarded trials (t(15)=-2.94, p=0.01).
source: This analysis indicated that changes in baseline pupil size indeed explained changes in representation strength in mOFC; as expected, this relationship was negative, such that increases in pupil size predicted decreases in representation strength. Interestingly, this relationship was limited to unrewarded trials (t(15)=-2.94, p=0.01)
evidence: This is a primary result from the pupil-brain analysis (GLM6).

claim: Within the subset of rewarded trials there was no relationship between changes in baseline pupil size and changes in representation strength (t(15)=0.37, p=0.71).
source: within the subset of rewarded trials there was no relationship (t(15)=0.37, p=0.71; difference between rewarded and unrewarded: t(15)=2.82, p=0.01; Figure 3b).
evidence: This is a result from the pupil-brain analysis (GLM6).

claim: The difference between rewarded and unrewarded trials in the relationship between pupil change and representation strength change was significant (t(15)=2.82, p=0.01).
source: within the subset of rewarded trials there was no relationship (t(15)=0.37, p=0.71; difference between rewarded and unrewarded: t(15)=2.82, p=0.01; Figure 3b).
evidence: This is a result from the pupil-brain analysis (GLM6).

claim: Increases in uncertainty occurred almost exclusively following reward omissions - on only 0.2% of core exploit trials (10/3833 trials over all participants) did uncertainty increase following a rewarded trial.
source: This is significant because (due to the 4-arm nature of the task and the fact that we included only exploitation trials in the analysis) increases in uncertainty occurred almost exclusively following reward omissions – on only 0.2% of core exploit trials (10/3833 trials over all participants) did uncertainty increase following a rewarded trial.
evidence: This is a result from the analysis of the task structure.

claim: The relationship between pupil dilation and change in representation strength seems to hold in cases where uncertainty is increasing, but not when it is decreasing.
source: Therefore the relationship between pupil dilation and change in representation strength seems to hold in cases where uncertainty is increasing, but not when it is decreasing.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the pupil-brain results.

claim: The result was no longer significant when shifting the pupil and OFC signals relative to one another in any direction (p>0.1 for all analyses).
source: To test the temporal specificity of the result, we shifted the pupil and OFC signals relative to one another and recomputed the effect. We found that the result was no longer significant when shifting the signals in any direction (p>0.1 for all analyses), suggesting the effect was temporally specific to change in pupil size predicting change in representation strength from the current trial to the next.
evidence: This is a result from a control analysis testing temporal specificity.

claim: The effect remained significant when regressing out value from the univariate signal before fitting the multivariate model (unrewarded: t(15)=-3.07, p<0.01; rewarded: t(15)=0.56, p=0.58; difference: t(15)=2.95, p<0.01).
source: This effect remained significant when regressing out value from the univariate signal before fitting the multivariate model, as discussed above (unrewarded: t(15)=-3.07, p<0.01; rewarded: t(15)=0.56, p=0.58; difference: t(15)=2.95, p<0.01).
evidence: This is a result from a control analysis.

claim: The result replicated in the mOFC ROI when including only explore trials in the analysis (unrewarded: t(15)=-2.38, p=0.03; rewarded: t(15)=0.97, p=0.35; difference: t(15)=-2.23, p=0.04).
source: Although we focus here on the exploitation phase, we found this result replicated in the mOFC ROI when including only explore trials in the analysis (Figure 3—figure supplement 2; unrewarded: t(15)=-2.38, p=0.03; rewarded: t(15)=0.97, p=0.35; difference: t(15)=-2.23, p=0.04).
evidence: This is a result from an additional analysis on explore trials.

claim: Performing the analysis on unrewarded exploit trials over the whole brain reveals a region relatively localized to mOFC.
source: Furthermore, performing the analysis on unrewarded exploit trials over the whole brain reveals a region relatively localized to mOFC (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is a result from a whole-brain analysis.

claim: Change in representation strength was more negative when change in pupil dilation was higher (t(15) = 2.72, p=0.02).
source: To illustrate this result further, we took the unrewarded exploit trials and looked at the change in representation strength in the mOFC ROI on trials separated according to a median split on change in pupil diameter. As expected, we found change in representation strength was more negative when change in pupil dilation was higher (Figure 3d; t(15) = 2.72, p=0.02).
evidence: This is a result from an analysis illustrating the main pupil-brain finding.

claim: On trials when evidence against the current belief is observed (unrewarded trials), the change in uncertainty in the neural model is predicted by changes in pupil diameter, suggesting a role for neuromodulation in control of uncertainty in neural models.
source: These results demonstrate that on trials when evidence against the current belief is observed (unrewarded trials), the change in uncertainty in the neural model is predicted by changes in pupil diameter, suggesting a role for neuromodulation in control of uncertainty in neural models.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the pupil-brain results.

claim: The relationship between pupil dilation and representation strength in mOFC is directionally specific to the process of increasing, not decreasing, model entropy.
source: The fact the relationship is specific to unrewarded trials suggests that the relationship between pupil dilation and representation strength in mOFC is directionally specific to the process of increasing, not decreasing, model entropy.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the pupil-brain results.

claim: ACC and adjacent preSMA activity was directionally sensitive to change in entropy.
source: This analysis identified activity in the ACC and adjacent preSMA that was directionally sensitive to change in entropy (Figure 3e, left).
evidence: This is a result from the fMRI analysis (GLM7).

claim: The greater the increase in entropy from the previous to current trial, the greater the activity in the ACC and surrounding regions of the dmPFC.
source: The greater the increase in entropy from the previous to current trial, the greater the activity in the ACC and surrounding regions of the dmPFC – that is, these regions were more active when entropy was increasing and less active when it was decreasing.
evidence: This is a result from the fMRI analysis (GLM7).

claim: ACC results are consistent with the observation ACC has been associated with the processing of feedback that should lead to changes of belief.
source: These results are consistent with the observation ACC has been associated with the processing of feedback that should lead to changes of belief (O'Reilly et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by a citation.

claim: ACC is one of the few cortical regions reported to have an afferent influence on the noradrenergic LC.
source: ACC is one of the few cortical regions reported to have an afferent influence on the noradrenergic LC (Jodo et al., 1998) .
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: ACC activity on a given trial predicted the change in baseline pupil size from that trial to the next.
source: When we controlled for this global effect by including mean activity across the grey matter as a co-regressor of no interest (GLM8), we observed a localized effect in ACC such that ACC activity on a given trial predicted the change in baseline pupil size from that trial to the next (Figure 3e, right; more activity in the brain associated with a greater increase in pupil dilation; corrected for multiple comparisons using permutation testing; p<0.05 at cluster forming threshold of p=0.001).
evidence: This is a result from the fMRI analysis (GLM8).

claim: This result is also present when conducting the analysis across all trials.
source: Although we focus on the exploit period, this result is also present when conducting the analysis across all trials (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a result from an additional analysis on all trials.

claim: There was no evidence for a direct relationship between ACC activity and changes in representation strength in mOFC.
source: Given that ACC activity predicts pupil dilation and pupil dilation predicts changes in representation strength in mOFC, we tested whether there was a direct relationship between ACC activity and changes in representation strength in mOFC. However, there was no evidence for such a relationship (activity extracted from an ROI defined on peak of the ACC effect from either GLM7 or GLM8 did not have a significant relationship with change in representation strength in mOFC; p>0.1 for all trial subsets tested).
evidence: This is a result from an analysis testing for a direct relationship.

claim: A very similar pattern of activity in medial prefrontal cortex was present when participants switched from exploitation to exploration.
source: Although we focus on the exploitation phase in which overt behavior was stable, it is worth noting that a very similar pattern of activity in medial prefrontal cortex was present when participants switched from exploitation to exploration (GLM2, Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a result from the fMRI analysis (GLM2).

claim: The activity observed in ACC is activity over and above that driven by changing response/option selection.
source: The activity observed in ACC in this analysis is activity over and above that driven by changing response/option selection (GLM2), which (by definition) occurs on the last trial of exploitation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the fMRI analysis (GLM2).

claim: The ACC effect is specific to exploration initiation, and was not observed when switching strategy from exploitation to exploration.
source: Note that this effect is specific to exploration initiation, and was not observed when switching strategy from exploitation to exploration (Figure 3—figure supplement 4), suggesting a particular role in disengaging from the exploited strategy.
evidence: This is a result from the fMRI analysis.

claim: Patterns of activity indicative of a probabilistic model of the environment were identified in the medial OFC.
source: We set out to investigate the mechanisms by which entropy in neural models of the world may be controlled, particularly mechanisms by which entropy may be increased. We identified patterns of activity indicative of a probabilistic model of the environment in the medial OFC.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: The hallmark of the probabilistic model in mOFC is that it has stronger representation strength for the currently selected option when model entropy is low.
source: The hallmark of this probabilistic model is that it has stronger representation strength for the currently selected option when model entropy is low.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: Changes in representation strength in medial OFC, over and above those predicted by the task model, were explained by change in pupil dilation.
source: Changes in representation strength in medial OFC, over and above those predicted by our task model, were explained by change in pupil dilation, a proxy measure for neuromodulator activity.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: Pupil dilation was predicted by activity in the ACC.
source: Pupil dilation was in turn predicted by activity in the ACC – a region also active when model entropy increased.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: That an internal model of the task is represented in mOFC is consistent with the proposal that this region represents the current location in task state space.
source: That an internal model of the task is represented in mOFC is consistent with the proposal that this region represents the current location in task state space (Wilson et al., 2014), and in particular represents information that is hidden to participants but required to solve the task (Chan et al., 2016; Schuck et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by citations.

claim: mOFC represents information that is hidden to participants but required to solve the task.
source: That an internal model of the task is represented in mOFC is consistent with the proposal that this region represents the current location in task state space (Wilson et al., 2014), and in particular represents information that is hidden to participants but required to solve the task (Chan et al., 2016; Schuck et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The fact that mOFC is the locus of the probabilistic model in the current task is probably due to the choice of task, as mOFC plays a key role in representing stimulus-action-outcome contingencies during model-based action.
source: The fact that mOFC is the locus of the probabilistic model in the current task is probably due to the choice of task, as mOFC plays a key role in representing stimulus-action-outcome contingencies during model-based action (Jones et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by a citation.

claim: Different stimulus or task domains could rely on probabilistic models represented in other, task relevant parts of cortex.
source: Different stimulus or task domains could rely on probabilistic models represented in other, task relevant parts of cortex.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about generalization.

claim: The representation observed in mOFC may reflect the online representation of option-reward contingencies required to guide choice and may not be where the option-reward contingencies are stored offline.
source: Furthermore, the exact nature of the representation we are interrogating in mOFC is an interesting avenue for future research. For example, it is possible the representation we observe here reflects the online representation of option-reward contingencies required to guide choice – for example, for online comparison – and is not where the option-reward contingencies are stored offline, which may be in another region such as hippocampus (Boorman et al., 2016) or striatum (Packard and Knowlton, 2002).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the nature of the representation, with citations.

claim: The striatum plays a key role in representing action-outcome associations.
source: The striatum also plays a key role in representing action-outcome associations, and indeed mechanisms for maintaining flexibility within these representations have been proposed (Franklin and Frank, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: In the current study we were unable to detect evidence of a probabilistic model in the striatum.
source: In the current study we were unable to detect evidence of a probabilistic model in the striatum.
evidence: This is a negative result from the study.

claim: Most theoretical work in the field of neuromodulation has focussed on noradrenaline.
source: We next sought evidence for a role of neuromodulatory systems in increasing uncertainty in such an internal model. Although most theoretical work in this field has focussed on noradrenaline, it should be noted that our results concern pupil dilation, not noradrenaline per se.
evidence: This is a statement about the literature.

claim: Pupil dilation depends on at least two neuromodulators (noradrenaline and acetylcholine), as well as other arousal-related factors.
source: Pupil dilation depends on at least two neuromodulators (noradrenaline and acetylcholine) (Joshi et al., 2016; Reimer et al., 2016), as well as other arousal-related factors, so our results cannot be linked directly to noradrenaline.
evidence: This is supported by citations and is a caveat about the interpretation.

claim: A large body of theoretical work has ascribed noradrenaline various functions relating to the modification of internal models.
source: A large body of theoretical work has ascribed noradrenaline various functions relating to the modification of internal models (changing gain (Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005), network resets (Bouret and Sara, 2005), and signalling unexpected uncertainty (Preuschoff et al., 2011; Yu and Dayan, 2005)).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: In one rodent study, increasing noradrenaline results in broader – less selective – tuning curves of auditory neurons.
source: In one significant rodent study, increasing noradrenaline results in broader – less selective – tuning curves of auditory neurons (akin to a network reset) (Martins and Froemke, 2015).
evidence: This is a finding from a cited study.

claim: By simultaneously measuring pupil size and an internal model in mOFC, we observed changes in pupil diameter predict increases in uncertainty in an internal model.
source: By simultaneously measuring pupil size and an internal model in mOFC, we observed changes in pupil diameter predict increases in uncertainty in an internal model, demonstrating a potential analog of this rodent work in humans performing complex decision-making tasks, and suggesting a broad role of pupil-linked neuromodulation in reducing selectivity of cortical representations.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings and their interpretation.

claim: ACC tracks changes in the certainty of beliefs.
source: We then asked which brain regions contain signals associated with changes in the certainty of beliefs and may be involved in regulating the pupil-linked neuromodulatory system. We found ACC tracked changes in the certainty of beliefs, consistent with observations that it monitors the outcomes of one's actions (Walton et al., 2004), predicts the updating of beliefs (Behrens et al., 2007), and is specifically engaged when internal models need to be updated (O'Reilly et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a summary of findings with supporting citations.

claim: ACC monitors the outcomes of one's actions.
source: We found ACC tracked changes in the certainty of beliefs, consistent with observations that it monitors the outcomes of one's actions (Walton et al., 2004), predicts the updating of beliefs (Behrens et al., 2007), and is specifically engaged when internal models need to be updated (O'Reilly et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: ACC predicts the updating of beliefs.
source: We found ACC tracked changes in the certainty of beliefs, consistent with observations that it monitors the outcomes of one's actions (Walton et al., 2004), predicts the updating of beliefs (Behrens et al., 2007), and is specifically engaged when internal models need to be updated (O'Reilly et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: ACC is specifically engaged when internal models need to be updated.
source: We found ACC tracked changes in the certainty of beliefs, consistent with observations that it monitors the outcomes of one's actions (Walton et al., 2004), predicts the updating of beliefs (Behrens et al., 2007), and is specifically engaged when internal models need to be updated (O'Reilly et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: ACC was particularly involved when uncertainty should increase, consistent with its role in exploratory behavior and information seeking.
source: ACC was particularly involved when uncertainty should increase, consistent with its role in exploratory behavior (Hayden et al., 2011) and information seeking (Stoll et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by citations.

claim: The present study provides evidence for a role of ACC in tracking changes in belief certainty, but was not designed to dissociate it from other roles ascribed to ACC, such as cognitive control and choice difficulty.
source: While the present study provides evidence for this role of ACC, it was not designed to dissociate it from other roles ascribed to ACC, such as cognitive control (Shenhav et al., 2013) and choice difficulty (Shenhav et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a caveat about the interpretation, with citations.

claim: The study double dissociates ACC from other regions representing an internal model (mOFC).
source: Rather, we double dissociate ACC from other regions representing an internal model (mOFC), and provide evidence ACC may broadcast information to such regions via neuromodulatory systems.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings.

claim: Recent studies have shown that activity of ACC neurons predicts pupil dilation and may temporally lead pupil-predicting LC activity.
source: Further, recent studies have shown that activity of ACC neurons predicts pupil dilation and may temporally lead pupil-predicting LC activity (Ebitz and Platt, 2015; Joshi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: It is anatomically plausible that ACC could influence belief uncertainty via the noradrenaline system.
source: Therefore it is anatomically plausible that ACC could influence belief uncertainty via the noradrenaline system, possibly amongst other routes.
evidence: This is an inference based on anatomical knowledge and previous findings.

claim: Both ACC and noradrenaline have been implicated in belief updating and setting the learning rate.
source: However, whilst both ACC and noradrenaline have been implicated in belief updating (Karlsson et al., 2012; O'Reilly et al., 2013) and setting the learning rate (Behrens et al., 2007; Nassar et al., 2012), evidence for their suspected (Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005; Karlsson et al., 2012; Nassar et al., 2012) coordination during tasks requiring belief updating has been lacking.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: ACC activity explained changes in baseline pupil dilation, over and above the effect of changes in uncertainty and mean brain activity.
source: Here we found ACC activity explained changes in baseline pupil dilation, over and above the effect of changes in uncertainty and mean brain activity.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: The noradrenaline system could offer a mechanism via which the computation of uncertainty of beliefs in ACC may be broadcast to internal models.
source: Whilst our pupil results cannot be linked directly to noradrenaline, they are compatible with the hypothesis that the noradrenaline system could offer a mechanism via which the computation of uncertainty of beliefs in ACC may be broadcast to internal models.
evidence: This is an interpretation and speculation based on the findings.

claim: An alternative explanation for the relationship between ACC and pupil dilation is that they are associated with a change in the drive to produce exploratory behavioural output.
source: An alternative explanation for the relationship between ACC and pupil dilation is that they are associated, not with a change in beliefs, but with a change in the drive to produce exploratory behavioural output.
evidence: This is a discussion of an alternative interpretation.

claim: Increasing noradrenaline release to the ACC has been associated with the output of stochastic behavior.
source: Indeed, increasing noradrenaline release to the ACC has been associated with the output of stochastic behavior (Tervo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: An account in which ACC activity and noradrenaline release only track a drive to produce stochastic behavioural output cannot account for the association between pupil dilation and the increase in model uncertainty recorded in mOFC, in the absence of any behavioural change.
source: However, an account in which ACC activity and noradrenaline release only track a drive to produce stochastic behavioural output, or to explore, cannot account for the association between pupil dilation and the increase in model uncertainty recorded in mOFC, in the absence of any behavioural change.
evidence: This is an argument against an alternative interpretation based on the data.

claim: Animal work provides causal evidence that noradrenaline reduces selectivity of cortical representations.
source: Further, the animal work described above (Martins and Froemke, 2015) provides causal evidence that noradrenaline reduces selectivity of cortical representations, supporting the proposed role for noradrenaline in reducing the strength of beliefs, in addition to its role of increasing stochastic behaviour (Tervo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Noradrenaline input to ACC alters the temperature parameter of a softmax choice model whereas noradrenaline input to internal models (mOFC) alters the option values.
source: This hypothesis can be summarized in terms of economic models of choice as arguing that noradrenaline input to ACC alters the temperature parameter of a softmax choice model whereas noradrenaline input to internal models (mOFC) alters the option values, resulting in behavioural stochasticity (Tervo et al., 2014) and entropic beliefs (present results), respectively.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation of the findings with a citation.

claim: The results suggest different neural mechanisms may be engaged when forming as compared to revising beliefs.
source: These results suggest different neural mechanisms may be engaged when forming as compared to revising beliefs, and that neuromodulatory systems may play a crucial role in implementing flexibility of internal representations during decision-making in humans.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Neuromodulatory systems may play a crucial role in implementing flexibility of internal representations during decision-making in humans.
source: These results suggest different neural mechanisms may be engaged when forming as compared to revising beliefs, and that neuromodulatory systems may play a crucial role in implementing flexibility of internal representations during decision-making in humans.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Twenty-two healthy human volunteers participated in the experiment.
source: Twenty-two healthy human volunteers participated in the experiment.
evidence: This describes the study sample.

claim: All participants were right-handed, aged between 20 and 31 (mean age: 26), and eight were female.
source: All participants were right-handed, aged between 20 and 31 (mean age: 26), and eight were female.
evidence: This describes the study sample.

claim: Three participants had to be excluded because of technical difficulties with fMRI.
source: Three participants had to be excluded because of technical difficulties with fMRI, and three had to be excluded from pupil analyses because of technical difficulties with eyetracking in the fMRI scanner.
evidence: This describes the study sample and exclusions.

claim: Three participants had to be excluded from pupil analyses because of technical difficulties with eyetracking in the fMRI scanner.
source: Three participants had to be excluded because of technical difficulties with fMRI, and three had to be excluded from pupil analyses because of technical difficulties with eyetracking in the fMRI scanner.
evidence: This describes the study sample and exclusions.

claim: The study was approved by a local University of Oxford ethics committee (ref: MSD-IDREC-C1-2013-171).
source: The study was approved by a local University of Oxford ethics committee (ref: MSD-IDREC-C1-2013-171), and all participants gave written informed consent.
evidence: This describes the ethical approval.

claim: All participants gave written informed consent.
source: The study was approved by a local University of Oxford ethics committee (ref: MSD-IDREC-C1-2013-171), and all participants gave written informed consent.
evidence: This describes the ethical procedures.
